sn11.12:1.3: _Maghavā_ (“bounteous one”) is a common epithet of Indra (eg. Rig Veda 3.39.09a, Atharva Veda 8.4.19a, Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 24.5.22). It is from the Vedic _magha_, “gift, bounty”. The name Māgha, with the same meaning, is a name of Sakka at [sn2.3](), while at [snp3.5:1.3]() a brahmin student Māgha asks about generosity. Finally, the good king of [mn83]() is named Maghadeva, “god of bounty”. The passage here attributes the name to his ancestry, but it goes on to praise his generosity.
sn11.12:2.1: _Purandara_ (“Fortbreaker”) is another epithet (eg. Rig Veda 1.102.7). The Buddha reforms it to _Purindada_ (“Firstgiver”) at [sn11.12:2.1](). But Indra’s generosity is long renowned: “He is the able one, and he will be able for us—Indra who distributes the goods” (Rig Veda 1.10.6).
sn11.12:3.1: _Sakka_ (_śakra_, the “able one”) was originally an epithet of Indra. |
sn11.12:4.1: Vāsava means “endowed with wealth” (_vasu_; see for example Rig Veda 1.9.9a _indraṁ vasupatiṁ_ “Indra, lord of wealth”). This passage, rather, plays on the word _āvasatha_ and calls him the “giver of a guesthouse”. Later Brahmanical texts enumerated eight Vasus, with Indra as their lord, who are reckoned among the thirty-three.
sn11.12:5.1: “Thousand eyes” is _sahassakkha_, more commonly _sahassanetta_ [sn11.9:2.3](), [snp2.12:5.4](), [thag21.1:58.4]()). In the Rig Veda it describes the sparkle of the Soma, perhaps alluding to its visionary effects (9.60, 9.65.7). It is in this context that Indra, along with Vāyu, is first called “thousand-eyed” (1.23.3). It is also used for Agni, the fire with eyes all around (1.79.12, 10.79.5).
sn11.12:6.1: They work together at the loom ([ud3.7:3.2]()). Sanskrit sources know his wife as Śacī (“the powerful”), daughter of the titan maiden Pulomā, who came to be known as Indrāṇī. _Śaci_ is a common descriptor of Indra’s deeds in the Rig Veda, from which it became his “wife”, with the same meaning as _sakka_ (Rig Veda 4.43.3). The Pali is probably a misspelling.
